To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the specificity of the thyrotropic response to glycoprotein hormones varies among vertebrate classes; 2) the specificity of this response is determined by the species of the pituitary hormone and the species of the thyroid gland, but not by the phylogenetic position of the species of thyroid gland relative to the species of pituitary hormone; 3) the specificity of thyroid responsiveness to glycoprotein pituitary hormones is determined by the evolution of the functional specificity of

the thyroid gland of amphibians, reptiles, and birds responded specifically to thyrotropin (TSH) purified from mammalian, sea-turtle, ostrich, or bullfrog pituitaries; that the three anuran (frog) species studied showed a high degree (greater than 10-fold) of specificity for bull-frog TSH, and that bull-frog luteinizing hormone (LH) exhibited low thyrotropin activity in the amphibian species tested.

the thyrotropins of mammals and reptiles are highly effective in stimulating the thyroid glands of amphibians; that the thyrotropic activities of amphibian gonadotropin preparations are attributable to their contamination with thyrotopin; and that bullfrog gonadotropics are more potent than its thyrotropin when tested on the thyroid glands of reptiles and birds.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the specificity of thyroid responses to pituitary hormones from various vertebrate classes.
the evolution of the specificity of thyroidal response to pituitaries hormones in vertebrate animals.
the evolution of the pituitary gland and its hormones in vertebrates and with the specificity of the pituitaries and their hormonal products in the control of endocrine glands of different species.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the thyrotropic response to heterologous glycoprotein hormones is not a general phenomenon in the vertebrates but that it is restricted to certain species and is not a common characteristic of the vertebrates as a whole.
the thyrotropin receptor of each species has evolved in a manner that has resulted in a high degree of functional specificity for the thyrotropins of its own class.
the specificity of thyroid responses to heterologous pituiary hormones is variable among species within the same vertebrate class and among species of different vertebrate groups.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the tetrapods, the thyrotropic response is generally specific for thyroxin, but that there are some exceptions to this generalization.
the thyroid gland is a highly sensitive and specific endocrine organ, which can be used for comparative studies on the evolution of the functional specificity of hormone-receptor interactions.
the specificity of thyroid stimulation by heterologous pituiary hormones is not a reliable indicator of evolutionary relationships between species.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the thyrotropin receptor is a highly conserved receptor that has evolved to be responsive to the same hormone across vertebrate species.
thyroid response to pituuitary glycoproteins is not universal and varies across species.
there is a high degree of conservation in the specificity of the TSH receptor across vertebrate classes.
